speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, multinational organizations hold conventions, summits, and often they seem to plod away in futile and seemingly non-productive efforts. But, sometimes their efforts are rewarded with substantive expressions of moral and philosophical principle; sometimes they come around to giving us some very specific examples of innovative ways to connect the capacity and will to give with the need to receive.
An occasion which gave recognition of both these great principles was the Brandt report that evolved out of the north-south dialogue. Within that report, as well as a series of important philosophic value statements found therein, there were specific ideas. Canada is not a large country. We cannot change the whole world. There is not a lot we can do. But when a specific suggestion such as this is brought forward, there are some specific areas where we can take grasp, run with and show the way. I am referring to the specific recommendation of the Brandt report regarding tripartite aid. The report described tripartite aid as follows:
The emergence of capital-surplus developing countries provide special scope for the establishment of projects on a basis of tripartite arrangements involving developing countries alone or in partnership with industrialized countries. Tripartite countries, including, when appropriate, industrialized countries, should be encouraged by nations with complementary resources such as capital and technology.
Adjournment Debate
To make my point meaningful, I wrote specific examples of need to receive, a technological capacity to give, and administrative capability and technological capability to carry out the projects which are so desired. There could be a multitude of combinations for this new suggested form of aid. This form of aid has advantages in that multinational corporations have become so large and cumbersome that they tend to be slow to act and require many other principles aside from the principle of need.
When one looks at organizations other than multinational organizations such as the United Nations, one takes specific blocs, such as the Commonwealth, OPEC and so forth. Often one cannot organize as freely, efficiently and quickly as one could if one took bilateral aid and extended it to trilateral aid or three-country aid. The specific example I have chosen is only one example. I chose the countries at random, Saudi Arabia being one of them. I chose this country because it has proven to be one of the most generous givers of foreign aid in the world through the recycling of their petro dollars. I chose Somalia because it is the fourth poorest country in the world. I have travelled there and seen the need with my own eyes. I chose Canada as the third country, a country with the capacity for technological exchange and administrative capacity to co-ordinate and deliver the same. This is a specific answer to an immediate problem. Somalia is a part of the African dry belt where there is tremendous drought and where there is malnutrition and starvation. Yet, just below the feet of those people starving and dying of thirst, 35 feet underground, is a plentiful supply of water. The land connot be dug by hand because it is sand and it caves in. Digging could be done if there were some cribbing and a solar pump. The water could be pumped to the surface. This would give the most basic element of life to help those people survive. Second, it could be used to aid in planting the fertile soil which requires just water and a little effort. The need could be met.
Canada has a great organization called CIDA, which has a billion of our dollars to spend. Canada is a country which has the technology and the capacity to deliver it. I find it hard to understand that I can travel to that country, as members opposite have, and see the needs there. It has been the subject of discussion in committee, the minister concurs, it is debated in this House, but still the need in Somalia cannot be met, bilaterally or trilaterally. I would like to see a specific example initiated by Canada.
I would like to conclude by saying that in his response, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) showed that he was concerned and interested in this matter. Prior to our Summit, I would like to see him establish a demonstration project in this area. I hope this area will be specifically addressed.
I thank you for your patience, Mr. Speaker, and I look forward to a positive response from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

March 31, 1981
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis Duclos (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most other industrialized countries in the western world, Canada tried in the last part of the seventies, both at bilateral meetings and in international assemblies, to encourage oil rich countries to share their new wealth with less fortunate developing countries and to co-operate with other donors and multilateral institutions to meet the priority development needs of these countries.
In 1980, Canada took part in the co-financing of 46 projects with a total value of $4.6 billion, its share coming to about $611 million, or 13 per cent of the total amount. Canada with OPEC Arab donors co-financed 18 projects with an approximate total value of $2 billion, in which the Canadian contribution amounted to about $350 million, or 17 per cent, and that of aid organizations of Arab countries which are members of OPEC, to over $750 million, or 37 per cent. In most cases, those were major projects for which the World Bank or some local development bank acted as the administrative or managing authority and Canada contributed financial assistance to an extent clearly defined as the Canadian participation to the project.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, Canada is participating in major bilateral aid projects in 34 developing countries, of which 12 or so are currently of interest to donor members of OPEC which are considering the possibility of giving them considerable aid, Canada would like to work more closely with the main aid bodies in the Arab country members of OPEC and the governments of developing countries with a view to broadening the scope and nature of its co-financing for the mutual benefit of all participants.
However, our attempts, so far, to improve the co-operation with the other donors lead us to believe that co-financing of worth-while projects is not easy and requires more time, efforts and administrative resources than usual bilateral projects. Industrialized countries, Arab donors and developing countries have objectives, policies, strategies and procedures in the field of aid that do not always coincide.
It seems that expanding the scope of co-operation in co-financing is hampered mostly by the lack of aid procedures and policies that are common to all participants and allow each one of them to achieve their own objectives at a reasonable cost compared with the benefits of the project. Most aid bodies in the Arab countries that are members of OPEC tend to concentrate their assistance in those countries where close ties already exist between politics, culture, economics and religion.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) has suggested on several occasions that we initiate demonstration projects in a special economic area such as energy and agriculture in a specific country, such as Somalia. While demonstration projects are sometimes a valuable tool to test an idea, a process or a product, we are not convinced, on the basis
of available information and our experience in joint financing, that such a demonstration project is necessary or even appropriate in the case of joint financing with oil-rich Arab countries of OPEC.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, if we proceed with our present bilateral discussions concerning programs, plans and problems in countries which are of mutual interest, I feel that in the light of our recent working experience with aid agencies in the Arab countries of OPEC, we will no doubt obtain positive results. Therefore, we intend to make greater efforts in that area.

CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-TESTING OF CHEMICAL DEFOLIANTS-MONITORING OF EFFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I am raising a matter which was raised some month ago, on January 23, 1981, concerning the spraying of agent orange in Gagetown in the province of New Brunswick. At that time I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) if her ministry had been made aware of this particular program, and if her ministry had monitored this program in terms of health effects to the surrounding population and the servicemen who were used for those tests.
I originally asked the question because agent orange has been under great suspicion in the United States as being a cause of various forms of cancer. The United States government has treated this connection with a great amount of seriousness. There are at least three major U.S. government groups studying the herbicide-related issues. Our concern was to find out what the Canadian government was doing and whether the Canadian government had the same concern. The concern about the spraying in the province of New Brunswick is not a new one. In fact, just prior to the release of the information that we had of the spraying of agent orange in New Brunswick, Dr. Cameron McQueen, from the province of Nova Scotia, had released a study which showed that there was an alarmingly high number of birth defects and retardation among children in New Brunswick.
As well, in part, I have in my hand a quote by the Minister of National Health and Welfare concerning the question of her department being informed about the spraying by the American army in Gagetown. She was asked by a reporter whether it bothered her that the federal defence department had never informed her department about the tests of agent orange at the Canadian Armed Forces base in Gagetown in 1966, and she is quoted to have said: "I can be shocked, but it won't help anybody."
There is general concern-and on my part, as well-as to how chemicals are treated in our society, how chemicals are used by governments and government agencies, that they are generally outdated and outmoded, and that the procedures, concerns and regulations must be brought up to date. We have
March 31, 1981

done things in the past out of ignorance which is just not excusable today. More and more, scientific information shows direct correlation between various forms of cancers and illnesses and the widespread use of deadly chemicals.
My concern is whether the Department of National Health and Welfare was informed by the Department of National Defence, and this springs from information that we have obtained and have read about the experience in the United States. I was concerned about whether Canadian servicemen knew what they were handling and whether, five or six years later, they could identify all sorts of symptons, or whether they were contracting cancer. Would they be in a position to seek some restitution from the government because they handled this particular chemical? As long as this situation was not made public and was not known to them, they could never be in a position to make a claim against the government.
At the time the minister indicated, and quite rightly, that she was not aware of the situation and that she would get as much information and details as possible. I will sit down in a few seconds because I want to give the government member ample opportunity to describe to the House exactly what steps the government has taken in the last two months to contact servicemen to perhaps change procedures so that when chemicals like agent orange are used in this country, the minister's department will know about it.
I look forward with interest to hearing what the government's spokesperson on this particular question will have to tell us tonight.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-TESTING OF CHEMICAL DEFOLIANTS-MONITORING OF EFFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been reported that in 1966 the Department of National Defence undertook spraying tests with chemical agents to test their effectiveness in reduc-
Adjournment Debate
ing the foliage cover over a tract of land belonging to the Gagetown base. At the time when these tests were being carried out, it was not known that 2,4-D and 2,4-5-T formulations could be contaminated with trace quantities of dioxin impurities. During the intervening years, better analytical procedures have permitted scientists to identify these impurities and increased knowledge of toxicology now allows characterization of some of their toxic properties.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) met with the minister of health for New Brunswick at the end of January at which time they discussed this issue. It was agreed that federal and provincial officials would co-operate fully in providing and exchanging all information and details concerning the spraying operation.
[Translation\
The minister of health of New Brunswick then gave the Minister of National Health and Welfare all available information on the spraying program on the Gagetown base. Officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare are now examining statistics on spontaneous abortions and miscarriages in the Sunbury riding, in New Brunswick, where the city of Gagetown is situated, for the years 1965, 1966 and 1967. The study will be completed in two or three weeks, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare will inform the minister of health of New Brunswick and the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) of the results. If they are positive, the advisability of supplementary research will be considered with the New Brunswick government in order to confirm the effects of some chemicals.
